utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-01-47-T, The Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning counsel. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Ekkehard Withopf, and the case manager Ruth Karper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. And the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel, Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel and Mirna Milanovic our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Residovic. And the other Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber would like greet everyone present in the courtroom members of the Prosecution, Mr. Withopf, Mr. Mundis. Defence counsel, the accused, and everyone else present Madam Registrar, the usher, the court reporter, and all those who are outside the courtroom and are contributing to the smooth running of these proceeds. As you are aware, we have to deal with the documents today. This issue will be dealt with on the basis of the subjects that were defined last week. The first subject about which the Prosecution will provide clarifications for the Trial Chamber concerns the origin of the various documents in all the binders we have at our disposal. And the Prosecution will explain to us how within the framework of its investigation they were in a position to obtain these documents. And as I said last Friday, these documents come from various sources, the main ones come from the Sarajevo archives, but there are also other sources for these documents, and the Prosecution will provide us with all the necessary relating to the origin of these documents. In that the Defence has contested some of these documents on the basis of unknown sources, that is to say, because some of the sources are unknown or can be put into question. So the Trial Chamber would like to be enlightened with regard to the origin of these documents. Likewise, the Prosecution was requested to provide the Trial Chamber with explanations of the authenticity of these documents, and we would like to be informed of the reasons for which the Prosecution believes these documents to be authentic. In addition, we should be informed to the extent this is possible about the chain of custody within BH, the chain of custody of these documents. We would like to be informed about this to the extent that it is possible for the Prosecution to do this. We would like to know the dates of the documents; we would like to know who the authors of the documents are, and how they were distributed within units because we have realised that for a number of documents there are some documents that don't contain details about who they were distributed to. This will enable us to have a clear idea about the origin and authenticity of the document concerned. After the Prosecution has presented its explanations, then the Defence will naturally also be in a position to state its position. And the Trial Chamber, if it is necessary, may also ask both parties any questions that are pertinent and relate to the documents. If the Prosecution refers to the documents, we have these documents before us, it would then suffice to indicate the number of the document concerned, the binder in which the document can be found, and that will then enable us to find the document that we have. This should make it easier to follow the proceedings. As I have said, the Defence will subsequently state its position in a general sense, the Defence should take or can take as much time as the Prosecution takes. But given the complexity of the issues to be dealt with the Defence will be granted leave to go beyond the time allocated if they deem that this is necessary. As far as going beyond the time allocated is concerned, this is a problem that arose yesterday. I would like to remind you that in order to clarify this issue, when we have witnesses or expert witnesses or anyone else who is testifying here, when conducting a cross-examination, you have one and a half times the amount of time given to the Prosecution. Sometimes there are problems, and it makes it necessary to go beyond the time allocated. We should be asked to grant you leave to go beyond the time allocated. We can then interrupt the Defence. We could say "you've used up your time, and you may no longer proceed." This would be unfortunate, but we can do this. To avoid this extreme, when preparing your cross-examination, bear in mind the time allocated to you, and if you encounter any difficulties, if you think that you will need more time, inform us in advance and provide us with reasons for this. If you have 20 documents you would like to tender, whereas the Prosecution only tendered one or two documents, tendering about 20 documents obviously will take a lot of time. You have to show the document to the witness; you need to give the witness time to read the document; it's necessary to hear what the Prosecution has to say about the document. So if such difficulties arise, do inform us of this. Having said this, I will now let Mr. Withopf take the floor. Mr. Withopf will provide us with clarifications concerning the first issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours. As indicated on Friday and today, the first issue to address are the sources of the documents. I will give a presentation on this issue following the following structure: First, I will address the main source of the Prosecution's document, in particular, the main source for the ABiH documents and the main source is obviously the Sarajevo collection. Afterwards, I will deal with the sources for the documents which stem from the Croatian State archive in Zagreb. And finally, I will address the documents which Your Honour, the Presiding Judge, specifically detailed last Friday. The presentation will address a number of issues the Trial Chamber raised on Friday and today. It will provide answers to quite a number of such issues. Afterwards, Your Honours, we are prepared to answer any questions to the extent possible. If I may, please, start with the Sarajevo collection. The Sarajevo collection is a document collection comprised of two distinct collections; namely, the Sarajevo Collection I and the Sarajevo Collection II. I will first address details in respect to the Sarajevo Collection I. The Sarajevo Collection I is a document collection comprised of about 49.375 pages of documents. Assuming that each page -- each document has an average 2.5 pages, the Sarajevo Collection I amounts to a total of about 22.000 documents. The -- about 50.000 pages of documents, Your Honours, were seized between 11 October and 19 October 2000 in three premises in Bosnia and Herzegovina; namely, number one, the ABiH main archive in Sarajevo, then located in the Ramiz Salcin barracks in Sarajevo, the search and seizure operation took place between the 11th and the 19th of October 2000. The second premises are the presidential archives in Sarajevo, then located in the Reisa Dzemaludina Causevica Street in Sarajevo. This search and seizure operation took place between the 11th and the 18th of October 2000. And finally, number three, the third premises were the premises of the 7th Mechanised Brigade. This is the military unit previously known as the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, headquarters in Zenica. This part of the search and seizure operation was done on the 13th and the 14th of October 2000. Mr. President, Your Honours, there is an important issue I wish to very briefly address in private session, if we please may go for one or two minutes in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam Registrar, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. 362 documents on the Prosecution exhibit list, Your Honours, stem from the ABiH archive. Two documents, namely, numbers 55 and 119, stem from the presidential archive. And seven documents, namely numbers, 56, 103, 104, 106, 308, 342, and 439 stem from the archives of the 7th Mechanised Brigade headquarters in Zenica. The documents on all premises, Your Honours, were seized as a result of a consensual search operation, consensual in the sense that the Bosnian authorities had been informed about the intended searches, had been requested to provide to the OTP access to the authorities mentioned, and the Bosnian authorities had given their consensus prior to the search operation. As a result of the consensus of the Bosnian authorities and the agreement reached with them, they, for each of the promises, the Bosnian authorities for each of the premises assigned a person responsible, responsible to support the representatives of the Prosecution and to sign over any, any documents to be signed as a result of the searches. The respective designated people were the following: For the ABiH archive, Major Suad Ramezic of the ABiH. He was the designated liaison officer. And Major Adem Omerkic, he was the chief archivist at the time. For the presidential archive, Mr. Bakir Sadovic. He was the designated from the Bosnian authorities, designated liaison officer. And finally, for the archive of the 7th Mechanised Brigade headquarters in Zenica, again, Major Suad Ramezic, Mr. Edin Obradovic, and the archivist, namely Mr. Smirko Sabahudin. If I may provide the Trial Chamber with some more detail on how the search and seizure operation was conducted. Mr. President, Your Honours, in October 2000, 11 representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor, including five investigators, two criminal analysts, one military analyst, two research officers, and of course language assistants, since the materials to be seized were in the B/C/S language. Ten language assistants were used for the search and seizure operation, these people under the direction and supervision of the then lead investigator in this case, namely, Mr. Stephan Obers; another investigator who is now the team leader of the Prosecution's investigation team in this case, namely Mr. Peter Hackshaw, and myself searched the document collections. In compliance with the conditions of the Bosnian authorities which at the time tried to avoid any public attention to the search operation conducted by the OTP, in compliance with the conditions, the document collections were searched during nighttime starting each and every day at about 1900 hours in the evening and lasting to about 4.00 to 5.00 in the mornings. This implies, Mr. President, Your Honours, that no other people than the designated officers, liaison persons of the Bosnian authorities and the mentioned representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor were at the respective premises at the time the searches were conducted. The document collections, Your Honours, were seized using a list of search criteria. This applies to all three premises. Such search criteria were identified based on the then knowledge of the broader investigation, including search criteria which are relevant for ongoing -- still ongoing investigations. If the Trial Chamber wishes us to do so, we can hand over the lists containing the search criteria used at the time, in October 2000, either on an ex parte basis or in a redacted version. On an ex parte basis or in a redacted version because these lists with the search criteria do, in addition to the search criteria specifically used for the investigations against the then three accused in the present proceedings, such lists reveal search criteria that relate to still ongoing investigations. If I may ask the Trial Chamber to provide some guidance in this respect. The documents which at the time, in October 2000, appear to fall within these search criteria were taken. Documents which appeared to not fit within these search criteria were left behind. A rough estimate, but I wish to underline this is a rough estimate only and it addresses a question raised by the Trial Chamber on Friday, a rough estimate is that about 2 per cent, 2 per cent of the documents of the ABiH archive, and about 5 per cent of the documents of the presidential archive were taken. This is a rough estimate only, Mr. President, Your Honours. A further question which was raised on Friday and also today by the Trial Chamber is the issue whether originals or copies were taken, if I may please briefly address this issue. The originals were taken at all three archive locations. Such originals are still held by the OTP in the chain of custody in the OTP's evidence vault. It is, however, the practice before this Tribunal with very rare exceptions that tendered into evidence are actually copies. Only if the Trial Chamber, however, wishes the Prosecution to produce the originals, we are in a position to do so. Copies of the originals were made and returned to the ABiH archive and the 7th Mechanised Brigade headquarters in Zenica between mid-November and early December 2001. During the search of the presidential archive, copies were made in the course of the search and seizure operation to replace the seized originals. Therefore, it was not necessary obviously to return copies to this location. In this context, Mr. President, Your Honours, it is important to note that in very few cases, no original was available in the archives; only a copy existed. In such instances, the Prosecution has the copy with the chain of custody as it was the only original, "original," available to us. Once the documents were taken, they were logged in a logbook which was signed each and every day. At the end of each and every day's search and seizure operation by the designated representative of the OTP and the person designated by the Bosnian authorities to do so. These logbooks, Mr. President, Your Honours, with the signed receipts are available, and we will hand them over now, the respective copies are available. We have three logbooks, obviously one for each of the three premises. And we will hand them over in a few seconds, please. Mr. President, Your Honours, there are copies for the Judges. There's a copy for the Chamber's legal officer. And there are obviously copies for Defence counsel as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a small question for you,

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: To the extent you are producing this logbook or these logbook, is there any trace of the document that you didn't retain for this particular trial but which are used for the purposes of other investigations and which may figure in these logbooks?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, to answer this question, yes, in these receipts there's obviously reference made to documents which may or may not be used in the course of ongoing proceedings, including investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you are producing these logbooks and a copy for the Defence, too, the Defence may find that there are other inquiries that are ongoing regarding other persons, and they may make such a conclusion on the basis of this document because there are documents that do not appear on your consolidated list. Could that be a problem for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, it won't be a problem. And I will address this issue in a few minutes. Defence actually has been given access to the full document collection, meaning that there's no additional information on the receipts. I will address this particular issue in a few minutes, please. Thank you, Mr. President. In the course of the searches, plans of the ABiH --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, a minor problem of a technical nature. You have provided us with copies, but I must note that unfortunately it is really difficult to read them. The quality of the copy is not very good. There are entire passages that are entirely illegible. When you photocopied these documents, the colour must have been almost spent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, you're obviously right, and I do apologise if the quality of the photocopies isn't that good as could be expected. And we will certainly be able to produce copies with the respective and necessary quality in the course of the -- today's court proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These logbooks, are you asking them -- are you asking that they be admitted into evidence so that we can give them an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, not at this point in time. It depends on the further discussions on these issues in the course of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In the course of the searches at the three premises mentioned, Mr. President, Your Honours, search plans of the ABiH main archive in Sarajevo and the ABiH -- and the archive within the headquarters of the 7th Mechanised Brigade in Zenica were made. Such search plans indicate as to where certain materials were found. These plans are available and we will hand them over now, please. Mr. President, I was just informed by my case manager that the whole bunch of materials was handed over at once, so the search plans are included in the materials you already got. For the ABiH 3rd Corps archive room, there's in addition a three-page explanation available, and it forms part of the materials handed over which, in addition, explains where on the various areas the binders containing the various documents were found. On 19 October 2000, Mr. President, Your Honours, all materials seized from all three archives were placed into large boxes and sealed with chain of custody forms. There were 30 such large boxes, and they were signed over to the head of the ICTY Sarajevo field office for the purpose of transporting the documents from Sarajevo to The Hague. On 22nd of October 2000, the documents with a truck were transported to The Hague where they arrived on the 25th of October 2000. Investigator, now the investigations team leader, Mr. Peter Hackshaw was present once the documents arrived, and Mr. Hackshaw has confirmed that they arrived intact and sealed. The chain of custody of these documents from the time they were seized until today can be shown if necessary. Each single one of the several documents has its own individual chain of custody log referred to as ERF, the evidence register form. If required, the Prosecution can for each and every document obtain the respective ERF from the evidence unit and produce them for the Trial Chamber. The documents upon arrival here in The Hague were then processed in the evidence unit in the usual manner; namely, they were ERNed. "ERN" stands for evidence registration number. It means that each of the documents was assigned a separate number. These are the numbers with the 16 digits one can see on each and every document the Prosecution is using. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. The documents were then scanned producing an image similar to an electronic copy but not searchable. Once scanned, an optical corrector recognition programme commonly referred to as OCR is then run over the scanned image which has the capacity to convert the scanned image into a text document which, depending on the quality of the original scanned image, is searchable. Mr. President, Your Honours, I do not want to go into the course of this presentation into much of the details of the pure technical side of the processing of such documents. A comprehensive overview of the procedure within the Office of the Prosecutor in relation to these documents is contained in a declaration which forms part of the materials which has been handed over. A declaration -- I do apologise, Mr. President. The declaration will be handed over separately. It's a declaration by Mr. Robert Reid. Mr. Robert Reid is the deputy chief of investigations, and he was the deputy chief of investigations at the time. This declaration on 1st of August 2001 was submitted in the course of the proceedings against Kordic and Cerkez, and the document -- the declaration will explain ion each and every detail the procedure within the Prosecution's evidence unit. This overview will also provide and will in addition provide the Trial Chamber with information on how the documents were handled within this unit. I don't think, Mr. President, Your Honours, I need to go in any more detail in that respect. If, however, required to do so, I would be in a position to explain further details. For the time being, I refer to the declaration of Mr. Robert Reid. I come now to an issue which Your Honours -- which Your Honour, Mr. Presiding Judge, addressed earlier on today in the proceedings. The full Sarajevo Collection I comprised of all documents was made available on 30 January 2002 to Defence counsel. This disclosure certainly went beyond the disclosure obligations of the Prosecution under Rule 66(A)(2) and Rule 68. One of the policy considerations at the time was the fact that it took the Prosecution some time to process the full collection, and Defence should not suffer in their trial preparation from this fact. The full Sarajevo Collection I was disclosed on that date, namely, the 30th of January 2002, on seven CDs for each Defence team, meaning fully searchable. I also wish to emphasise that due to the fact that these documents were all in B/C/S, the Defence having B/C/S speakers amongst them, was certainly earlier in a position than the Prosecution to analyse the document collection provided to them. I also wish to inform the Trial Chamber that the Prosecution on three occasions provided Defence with thousands of translations of documents which stem from the Sarajevo collections. If I now, Mr. President, Your Honours, with your permission, may proceed with details in respect to the Sarajevo Collection II. The Sarajevo Collection II is comprised of 610 documents which result in approximately 1.000 pages of documents. These 610 documents were again as a result of a consensual search, were seized between the 15th and 19th of April 2002. Again, this search was not only focussing on the two accused in the present proceedings, but also included additional, ongoing investigations. At this point in time, in April 2002, only the ABiH archive which was located at new premises compared to October 2002 [sic], the ABiH archive was now located in the Halida Nazecica Street 3 in Sarajevo at this point in time this archive was searched. Different from the first search and seizure operation, only copies - this time only copies - were taken. The originals remained in the archive. The respective logbooks, and again, the logbooks with the signed receipts, do form part of the bundle we handed over earlier on today. The person assigned by the Bosnian authorities to support the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor and to sign the receipts this time was Captain Miralem Duranovic from the ABiH. 35 such documents or 35 documents on the Prosecution's exhibit list stem from the Sarajevo Collection II; namely numbers 165, 290 to 296, 298 to 300, 302 to 305, 309, 316, 322, 325, 327, 328, 333 to 337, 3 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I do apologise. I will continue with 337, 382, 415, 422, 424 to 427, 432, and 435. Mr. President, Your Honours, this concludes the portion of my presentation which has to do with the Sarajevo collection. A second main source of the documents which form part of the Prosecution's exhibit list were received from the Croatian State archives in Zagreb. And I make a reference to the further detailed consolidated exhibit list in which all these documents are indicated. In respect to the Croatian State archives in Zagreb, I wish to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the testimony of Mr. Marko Prelec in the course of the trial against Martinovic and Naletelic, commonly referred to as Tuta and Stela. Mr. Prelec is a member of the OTP. He is a research officer and he testified for three days as a Prosecution witness on exactly the issue of how documents were obtained from the state archive in Croatia, and he testified on 25th of October 2001, 26th of October 2001, and 31st of October 2001. We are going to hand over copies of this public testimony right now. This testimony, as you will see, Mr. President, Your Honours, this testimony covers the exact issues in question here, and the transcript which will be handed over in a few seconds includes the examination-in-chief, the cross-examination by the Defence for Tuta and Stela, the re-examination of the Prosecution, and all questions asked by the Judges. The main issues this Trial Chamber may be interested in were addressed by the witness during the examination-in-chief on 25th of October 2001. The transcripts just handed over, Mr. President, Your Honours, will provide the Trial Chamber with a very comprehensive picture on this source, this source which is identified as the Croatian State Archive. Very briefly, for ease of reference in the course of today's discussion, I wish to summarise the most relevant portions of the testimony of the Witness Prelec as follows: In April and May 2000, after a series of RFAs, meaning requests for assistance, and binding orders by a number of Trial Chambers, the Croatian authorities provided representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor limited access to the archive which is colloquially referred to as the HVO archive. In summer 2000, the Croatian authorities provided extended access to the HVO archive and to other archives which came from the custody of various parts of the Croatian Ministry of Defence. Part of this big archive formed the HVO materials, obviously the bigger part. The archive, however, included to a limited extent also ABiH materials. The archive, as Your Honours will see from the testimony of Mr. Prelec, the archive consists of over 10.000 items, an item being a binder or a box containing loose materials. The archive is not a public archive. Access to this archive is regulated by the Croatian authorities and, following respective requests, is given to the same extent to both Prosecution and various Defence teams. In practice, and this is in compliance with an agreement between the Office of the Prosecutor and the Croatian authorities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, among the documents you have handed over to us, you made copies for the Judges and the Defence, but have the accused received copies? It appears that General Kubura doesn't have a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, since these -- to be very clear, the accused haven't received copies. They have not received copies. And the materials are obviously in the English language only, which the accused at least to the knowledge of the Prosecution don't understand. Therefore, at this junction the Prosecution didn't consider it being necessary that these materials be handed over and be translated into B/C/S to the accused. In respect to the testimony of the Witness Prelec, however, if the Trial Chamber requests the Prosecution to do so, the respective audiotapes of the court session in the B/C/S language can be handed over to the two accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I'm about to finish this presentation on the Sarajevo archive and the Croatian State Archives in Zagreb. However, I wish to very briefly address the issue on how in practice the documents from the Croatian State Archives were received. In compliance with an agreement between the Office of the Prosecutor and the Croatian authorities, the OTP receives copies - receives copies - of the materials, not the originals, as follows: A representative of the OTP examines an item, as mentioned, a binder, for example, identifies certain documents, marks them with a sticker, hands the binder to a designated archivist designated by the Croatian authorities, and the archivist takes care that the representative of the Prosecution on the next day receives copies; again, copies, not the originals of the documents he had marked. Once this is done, the documents are handled by the ICTY field office in Zagreb. They are indexed and summarised and finally they are ERNed. As a quality control, the copies received from the archive are checked by the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor against the lists that were made when the binder was handed over to the designated archivist for photocopying. Mr. President, Your Honours, I think that at this point in time, Defence may wish to address the issues which have been addressed by the Prosecution in the course of this presentation. And I would suggest that once this is done, I will for the Prosecution provide further information on the exhibits which Your Honour, Mr. Presiding Judge, have specifically addressed in the course of the last Friday's court session. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. Before giving the floor to the Defence, I shall summarise as follows what you told us: You have explained to us that the documents which were in the possession of the Prosecution were collected through official channels which entailed cooperation with the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the authorities of Croatia. Concerning the archives, there was Sarajevo I and Sarajevo II collections. You have explained to us that as for the archives of Sarajevo I, you are in possession of the originals. As for the Sarajevo II collection, the originals remained in the location, and you made photocopies. This procedure resulted from a search carried out during the night so as not to cause any public disorder. You mentioned the perfect cooperation of the archivists and those officials that cooperated with members of the OTP. Then these documents were registered in conformity with judicial procedure. And each document was given a number. And these documents, as a result of the research procedure, do not allow for any calling in question the regularity of the procedure applied in making that collection. Regarding the State archives of Croatia in Zagreb, you have indicated that contrary to the Sarajevo I collection, you were not able to obtain originals, but only copies. And that the procedure of obtaining copies was carried out in the following manner: A representative of the OTP reviewed the documents, marked them with a sticker attached to the document that needed to be photocopied. The next day, the responsible archivist provided copies. The investigator checked that the copy corresponded to the original document. And it was under those conditions that you carried out what you called "quality research." In support of this procedure, you support -- you have handed over the testimony of an official from the OTP, Mr. Marko Prelec, who testified in the Martinovic-Naletelic case. The testimony took three days, and we have been provided with the totality of that testimony in English. But there's no problem for providing the accused with that testimony in their own language. And this official described over a period of three days the procedure applied. That would be a summary of your presentation. So we have the Sarajevo I and the Sarajevo II collection, as well as a collection from the archives of Croatia. I wish to thank you for your very interesting presentation. And before continuing regarding the other sources, have the Defence in view of what has been said any observations to make. So I give the floor now to Mr. Bourgon and Madam Residovic. I don't know who will speak. Mr. Bourgon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Mr. President, at this stage we have heard from the Prosecution explanations and arguments regarding the sources of the documents that they wish to tender into evidence in the course of these proceedings. When the Chamber identified the five topics that needed to be addressed during these hearings on the admissibility of documents, there were other issues that needed to be addressed under the broad topic of the source. The Chamber then mentioned that the source included the origin of the document, and also a number of precise questions were addressed to the Prosecution regarding those documents. At this stage, Mr. President, we would prefer to hear the arguments of the Prosecution on the other questions because for us, the question of Sarajevo archives and Zagreb archives only constitute a small part of the submissions that we wish to address this morning. There are other much more important questions, and we would prefer to hear the Prosecution first on the other questions addressed to them, and then to make our global presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. I turn now to the other Defence teams and specialists for documents. Mr. Dixon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I agree with Mr. Bourgon. Our dispute about the documents has never been focussed on the legality of the search itself or what happened after the search, the chain of custody that the Prosecution then initiated. Our main point of challenge has always been what happened before the documents got into the archive. How did the documents originate and how did they get into the archive? That is the key question for us. So what we've addressed up until now is not in dispute, as Your Honour has said, an entirely regular procedure appears to have been followed. And what we wish to focus on is what happened before the documents arrived in the archive. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dixon. Mr. Withopf may take the floor again. He will certainly be continuing. The Trial Chamber notes that at this point in time, the Defence has no comments to make regarding the manner in which the Prosecution obtained these documents. utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence would like to make a few observations regarding the admissibility of documents as requested by the Chamber and following instructions provided last week. First of all, Mr. President, the Prosecution was asked to fill in certain gaps, to answer certain questions regarding the first topic, and that is the topic of origin or source. The Prosecution was asked to speak of the origin or the source of the documents. Also, the Prosecution was asked to tell us the way in which the documents were obtained. And there was a specific question also, and that is why the Defence had certain documents which the Prosecution did not appear to have in their possession. I think that these three questions have been replied by the Prosecution. However, there are two matters of very great importance for the Defence for which answers were not provided. The Chamber asked the Prosecution to tell us why they believed that the documents which they were producing should be -- to be admitted into evidence were authentic documents. And we have not received a reply to that question by the submissions made by my learned friend. Also, the Chamber asked the Prosecution to address a specific question regarding military orders. That is, the drafting of military orders. Were they verbal orders, written orders, or other types of orders? And how those orders were distributed. With all due respect, Mr. President, we feel that the Prosecution has not responded to this question. A second remark before I proceed has to do with the five topics chosen by the Chamber which in the opinion of the Defence are very useful, both for us, for us to prepare the Defence case, but also for the Chamber, regarding the admissibility of documents. Mr. President, in our view, more than one of the five criteria are necessary. And in some cases, all five criteria need to be fulfilled in our opinion in order to be able to decide on the admissibility of documents. Today, we have addressed three of those five criteria; the first, the source, and a bit later the criterion regarding technical problems as well as the question of relevance. However, Mr. President, with respect, we feel that it would be necessary to wait for the assessment and the submissions of both parties regarding Topics 5 and 6 before being able to take a position regarding the admissibility of certain documents. In agreement with the Rules of Evidence and Procedure and the position taken by the Chamber concerning the admissibility of documents, and that is my third observation this morning, the submissions presented by the Defence are limited to the admissibility of documents. The arguments that we will present today do not refer to the weight which may be subsequently given to the admitted documents, and no reference is made either to the inculpatory or exculpatory nature of those documents. We will simply limit ourselves to the questions put by the Chamber; that is, the criteria that have a direct bearing on the admissibility of documents. To do that, it would be useful to briefly refer to the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. And I will begin with the decision in the Tadic case, a case bearing number IT-94-1, and entitled "Decision on the admissibility of hearsay evidence," a decision dated the 5th of August 1996. In this decision, the Chamber felt that it was implicit in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and especially in Rule 89(C) that the admissibility included the criteria of reliability or trustworthiness, that this was a component which needed to be judged when a document is declared admissible. I will refer to another decision in the Delalic case, a decision dated -- that decision is dated the 19th of January 1998, and it is entitled "Decision on the motion of the Prosecution for the admissibility of evidence." In this decision, Mr. President, the Chamber found that the only two criteria that needed to be assessed when determining the admissibility of a document was, according to Rule 89(C), relevance and probative value. The Chamber defined relevance at the time as being the relationship that may exist between two facts. The Chamber also used as -- for probative value the following definition: The tendency of a piece of evidence to establish the submission, the claim made by a party, and for which it is being tendered. This is a loose translation because the text I was working with is in English. In the same ruling, the Chamber expressed its agreement with the decision in the Tadic case of the 5th of August 1996, according to which it is implicit in the Rules of Evidence and Procedure that the trustworthiness of a document is an inherent component of relevance and probative value, for it is quite clear that if evidence is not trustworthy, it cannot be relevant, nor can it have probative value. So again, this is a free translation of an English text. The Chamber continued in saying that this assertion regarding trustworthiness being an inherent component does not make it necessary for the Chamber to determine the authenticity of a document or the identity of the author, or the credibility of evidence. And this in the admissibility stage. The Chamber offered two reasons for this: The Chamber first said that the authenticity of a document as well as proof of the identity of its author were elements which would be of greater importance when the Chamber assesses the weight to be attached to each piece of evidence, which means subsequent to admissibility. The Chamber also took a position regarding the standard for the admissibility of documentary evidence which shouldn't be too high because generally speaking, documents tendered by a party are not designed to prove the guilt or innocence of an accused; but rather, to establish a context and complete the image presented by the totality of the evidence collected. Consequently, Mr. President, the Chamber in the Delalic case said the more a piece of evidence contributes to establishing a fact, the higher the standard should be at the admissibility stage. I come then, Mr. President, to the decision in the Brdjanin and Talic case. It is a case with the number IT-99-36, a decision of the 15th of February 2002 entitled, and I'll quote it in English "decision on the standards governing the admission of evidence." In this decision, Chamber II made the following ruling: First of all, it said, regarding documentary evidence, when a question of reliability is posed, it should not be considered as a first stage separate from the admissibility stage. Also in the opinion of the Chamber, one should not confuse the verification of reliability prima facie with the proof. This seems to go -- to be in contradiction with the arguments of the Defence. Also, the Prosecution needs to establish the relevance and probative value of a document for it to be admitted into Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. evidence. It is not necessary, however, to prove the authenticity or the identity of a document, nor even the source. A very important decision which is to some extent in contradiction with what we have said so far. Also, the Chamber said at the end that it could ask the Prosecution to provide a minimum of proof which would be sufficient to establish the reliability of an evidence prima facie if a document requires such proof. These criteria which we have found in the documents addressed to the Chamber, and this is attached to our submissions, that is the necessity to establish a prima facie case for reliability if a document requires such proof. Secondly, in this way, we read the decision of the Chamber dated the 23rd of April according to which the Prosecution was requested to present their submissions regarding the authenticity of documents, that is, the reason for which the Prosecution says that the documents they are producing are authentic. And regarding the preparation of military order, their signature attached to the -- and the affiliation with a particular military command. The position of the Defence as we have said many times is that a prima facie reliability of documents goes to the very heart of the topics established by the Chamber, particularly the topic of source. For us, reliability consists of four elements: The two principal elements being the provenance, or the origin, that is, where the document was drafted; and secondly, the criterion of safeguarding the document, that is, from the moment it was created and -- to the moment it was produced in court, was that document the same? Was it altered in any way to modify the weight that may be given to it subsequently? The third stage, Mr. President, is the criterion of authenticity. Is a document authentic? Mr. President, we consulted various opinions in an effort to present a clear and transparent and simple definition for the authenticity of a document. In Black's Law Dictionary, and in the Robert dictionary, the following criteria appear to be mentioned: "The authenticity of a document requires that we know who is the author that the document is attributed to." Let me rephrase that. A document which establishes who the author is or a document that is in conformity with its appearance. A contrario, a document that is not false, that is not suspect, and a document that is not uncertain. Regarding the question of reliability for us, this criterion is applied in a specific manner to all orders which may have been issued by various military units that were present on the ground. The authenticity of documents in our view, Mr. President, requires an evaluation of the signature on the document, who is the author of the document, not to prove the identity, but if a document uses a block signature, Major X, it is necessary for us to be able to say that the document regardless of the truthfulness of its contents is indeed a document issued by Major X. The sending of the document is also proof of its authenticity. In other words, to whom it was addressed, then how it was used. The reception of a document is also evidence or an element of evidence which could assist the Chamber in determining its authenticity. The drafting is also very important. Who drafted the document? Who signed it? And who authorised it? The closeness of the document to the accused is also an important factor. By way of an example, a document produced by a headquarters which has absolutely no link with the unit, the place of work of the accused in our view would reduce the authenticity of the document. Of course, together with certain other criteria. The number on a document can also be used to judge its authenticity. We have to have evidence of the system of numbering of documents that was used at the time. The way in which documents were drafted and why a document was drafted. The instructions given to the person who drafted the document, as well as the sources used by that person. So, Mr. President, at this stage, those would be our main remarks regarding the source, for the source includes this element of reliability, also the criterion of authenticity. And to address the matter in a more specific manner category by category, the documents produced by the Prosecution will be addressed category by category. First of all, Mr. President, there are documents that come from the archives. My colleague from the Prosecution has provided us with information about documents that come from the Sarajevo archives, the Zagreb archives, and the 7th Brigade archives. I don't think that my colleague mentioned documents from the archives of the Prosecutor's office in Travnik. But, Mr. President, as far as the question of archives is concerned, the Prosecution has submitted a number of arguments. And they stated that on the basis of the archives from which documents were taken, from that point in time up until a point in time the documents arrived in the Tribunal, we have various sorts of information. Mr. President, we have the document, its origin. The origin of the document is important if we want to establish a minimum of reliability. If we are to believe that the document is authentic, it is necessary to know who produced the document. It's necessary to know what the purpose of the document was. And it's necessary to know whether the document was actually used before it ended up in the archives. A while ago we mentioned, or rather my colleague mentioned the possibility of having the three archivists appear before the Chamber. The Defence doesn't want to waste any time, Mr. President. We don't want to slow down the proceedings. What my colleague suggested is quite acceptable. We could discuss this with the Prosecution. We could accept this possibility. Nevertheless, what is important in our opinion is that at the time the document was created, how was that document preserved within the 7th Brigade, in the 3rd Corps headquarters or another military unit, and how did this document get to the archives, arrive in the archives? But first of all, it is necessary to examine the document itself. The next category of documents, Mr. President, concerns documents for which no sources have been indicated. In our opinion, Mr. President, a document for which the Prosecution can't tell the Trial Chamber about the source, if that is the case, the document should not be admitted because there is no proof of the reliability of such a document, not even a prima facie proof, not even prima facie proof of its authenticity. My colleague mentioned documents that came from the Blaskic case, documents which were filed in another case. Mr. President, there are no rules contained within the Rules of Procedure and Evidence that deal with the admissibility of documents that were admitted into evidence in another case. It's our opinion, Mr. President, that if the Prosecution wants to tender a document from another case, it should do so in the same manner that it tenders all other documents. The Prosecution should not assume that the document should be admitted in this case. If the document comes from the Blaskic case or from another case, it nevertheless has to satisfy the same conditions. In such a case, the Prosecution, pursuant to Rule 92 bis (D) could submit part of the testimony of the person through whom the document in question was tendered. That's one example. There are other manners that could be followed. A document admitted in the Blaskic case should have a sufficient amount of reliability in order to be admitted in this case. The following category of documents, Mr. President, concerns the documents that were provided to the Prosecution by witnesses on a number of occasions. My colleague has referred to documents provided by witnesses or by individuals who at some point in time were potential witnesses. Nevertheless, Mr. President, we would like to point out that in certain cases with regard to documents that the Prosecution wanted to tender into evidence, the documents were obtained by witnesses who have testified before this Chamber, and the documents weren't produced on such occasions. We believe, Mr. President, that if the Prosecution receives a document from a witness who appears before this Trial Chamber, and if the Prosecution doesn't bother to present the document, tender the document into evidence through this witness, this document shouldn't be admitted following the testimony of the witness concerned. Mr. President, as far as the documents obtained from governments are concerned, a document obtained from a government must likewise satisfy certain conditions in order to be admitted into evidence in this specific case. The document obtained from a government in the Defence's opinion is different from a document obtained from the archives of the same government because when this document is provided, it is provided for a very specific reason. As the Trial Chamber said quite rightly last week, either it's the Prosecution who requested the document or the government offered to provide the document. In both cases, this is important information. My colleague mentioned earlier on that it is very likely, or to use the English words, it is very likely that the documents concerned were obtained following requests for assistance. That's what he termed the RFA, the request for assistance. We believe that for the document to be tendered into evidence in the course of these proceedings, this request for assistance should be attached to the document. The request made by the Prosecution in order to obtain the document. Or, on the contrary, if the document was offered by the government itself, it's necessary to know on what occasion and why the document was provided to the Prosecution. The following category of documents that I would like to deal with, Mr. President, concerns documents from private sources, from persons who were met on different occasions either in the field by investigators or at other points in time. Mr. President, we need to know the source of these documents, and we need to know the reason for which the document was provided to the Prosecution. These are two of the criteria that have to do with the admissibility of a document. We then have documents from the UN, Mr. President. The Trial Chamber has noted that for all these documents, the Defence never contested any of these documents. UNPROFOR documents haven't been contested by the Defence either. All the documents from the ECMM mission haven't been contested by the Defence either. Why? Because we believe that these documents satisfy the criteria established; that is to say, we have on the basis of the documents itself, on the evidence presented here, we have the document. We know how the document was drafted. We know the context within which the document was produced. And likewise, we know the source of the documents. All these details, in addition to the proof established in the course of the proceedings, allow us to believe that these documents are reliable. And when we say that a document is reliable, Mr. President, and I'll go back to what I said at the beginning, we mean that the document is reliable because it can be used by the Trial Chamber. But this has nothing to do, no relation to the weight that may be attached to the document. The weight attached to the document is to be assessed subsequently by the Trial Chamber. Mr. President, with regard to certain comments on various types of documents, various types of comments were made by the Prosecution. First of all, Mr. President, we have documents that come from the 3rd Corps. There are orders that come from the 3rd Corps. These orders were established in what was probably a standard manner in the military, but we don't know anything about this. We know that a military document, and now I'm referring specifically to military orders, we know that in the case of a military document, there is a person who issues an order, there's a person to whom the order is addressed, and the order has a certain content. The person issuing the order appears in the document itself. There's the block signature at the bottom of the document, if there is such a signature naturally. It's important to know whether this document was really an order issued by the person whose signature is at the bottom of the document. It's not a matter of proving who the author of the document is, but it's a matter of establishing sufficient indicia for reliability. In order to do so, it's necessary to establish that if a document is being tendered and bears the printed signature of the author, it's necessary to have indicia that shows that this order is actually an order issued by the accused. There are a number of ways of verifying this, either on the basis of the signature or on the basis of the signature of another person who may have been authorised to sign orders on behalf of the accused, or through other means. Nevertheless, Mr. President, in order to have the necessary proof concerning the drafting of orders or the manner in which orders were drafted or the manner of which this was established in headquarters, this is necessary if a document is to be admitted. The Prosecution has the burden of proof to show the Trial Chamber how a document was drafted in order for us to know whether the document we have, with the printed signature, with the signature that we can sometimes identify and sometimes can't identify, this is necessary in order to establish whether it's really an order that was issued by the person whose signature is contained in the document. The document will only be considered authentic if the document was used. If it's a document that should remain internal, it's necessary to identify the factor -- to identify the fact that the document was to remain in headquarters. If it's an order, it's necessary to know who the order was addressed to. This is necessary in order to have a minimum of probative value which would allow the Trial Chamber to use the document, whatever the purpose may be. So the problems we have are of several kinds. There are documents that have no signature. In our opinion, this constitutes indicia that the document is not reliable, unless we have information on duplicata which the Trial Chamber explained last week. Then we have documents for which we don't know whether they were sent or not. An order addressed to someone but we do not know whether the person received the order or whether the order was actually sent to the person. In other words, Mr. President, did the document just remain in the headquarters without any effect, or did it serve a purpose? This is an important criteria that has to be assessed when deciding on the admissibility into evidence of the document. In our opinion, the Trial Chamber has noted that when the document contains a signature that hasn't been identified, when a document doesn't mention the addressee or whether it was received, there is no proof about this, these are arguments that we will address tomorrow and have to do with Rule 89(D). Mr. President, the Trial Chamber has also noted that when the signature of the accused is identifiable on a document, in some cases, if there's no proof that the document was sent or received, the document was admitted. Naturally, nothing was said about the weight that would subsequently be attached to the document concerned. The next category of documents, Mr. President, concerns the documents that come from outside the 3rd Corps. A document comes outside the 3rd Corps, is exterior to the 3rd Corps if it was produced by a unit that has no link with the 3rd Corps as far as the usefulness of the document is concerned. As an example, Mr. President, a document that may have been sent by one of the operational groups attached to the 3rd Corps, a document sent to one of the brigades that is under this corps, under this operational group, I apologise. And if there is no mention in the document stating that a copy was mentioned to the 3rd Corps for its information, or if on the document the headquarters of the 3rd Corps was mentioned as one of the addressees on the document, the same criteria applicable, Mr. President. Who the document was sent to, whether it was received, et cetera. We think the standard should be even higher in this case because it's a document that doesn't even concern the accused who worked in the 3rd Corps headquarters. What did the accused know about this document, a document of this type, unless we know who it was sent to, who received it and who authorised it. In such a case, it could be used to prove something against the accused. But if we don't know who signed the document and if we don't know who it was sent to and if we don't know who receive the document, if we don't know why the document was drafted, in such a case such a document that comes from outside the 3rd Corps requires us to proceed with a lot of caution before we use such a document as evidence against the accused. The following category of documents I would like to address, Mr. President, are documents that come from the HVO. These documents come under the heading of documents that come from outside the 3rd Corps. Nevertheless, there's an important difference to be made here -- important distinction to be made here. The HVO was the enemy of the 3rd Corps, the enemy of the BH army. A document which was drafted, which was produced within the HVO and which is never received by the accused, a document that the accused were never familiar with, before using such a document, indicia of reliability must be even higher with regard to the signature, the person who received the document, the person who sent the document, and the drafting of the document. In the course of these proceedings, we have already seen various evidence that concern propaganda campaigns. A document drafted by the HVO which, for example, comes under the heading of the addressee made mention the European Mission, it may mention the British Battalion, it may mention the 3rd Corps headquarters, and then a list of persons who it was addressed to internally. In such a case, such a document should have been sent to the accused. But if we don't have any details that show that the document in question was sent or received by one of these persons, we don't have the minimum indicia of reliability which would enable us to use this document against the accused because this document may very well have been written within the framework of a propaganda campaign or as internal evidence, and it may have been produced for a very specific reason. If the Trial Chamber has no other information, in such a case, in our opinion, it should not admit such a document into evidence. On the other hand, in one of the addressees, for example, if the ECMM received a copy of the documents, in our opinion, that would be sufficient to say that the document has an indicia of reliability that is quite sufficient. And in such a case, the Judges could adopt the document, and the document could be admissible. But when assessing the weight, then it's necessary to know whether we have proof that the accused received the document in question. But that would be at a subsequent stage. Mr. President, thus referring to a document sent to a number of addressees, and we don't know if any of the addressees received the document; we don't even know whether the document concerned was sent. The following category of document, Mr. President, concerns operational logs. Some of the documents presented by the Prosecution to be admitted into evidence are logs which were kept on a daily basis in the headquarters. These logs were certainly established on the basis of a well-known modus operandi within the headquarters itself. Nevertheless, we do not know about this. We need to have knowledge about this in order to have a minimum indicia of reliability. We need to know not the identity of the person, but we need to know the position of the person who established the log held. We need to know what the person's instructions were. We need to know what the sources used were. We need to know the sources used when compiling the log. We need to know the conditions in which it was compiled. Was it on the basis of information received over the telephone? Or on the basis of information received over the radio? Or information received through people who visited the 3rd Corps? Was everything noted down or not? And in addition, Mr. President, such documents are handwritten documents. This is an issue that we will address a little later. These operational logs, Mr. President, in our opinion must be presented in their entirety. If the Prosecution wants to tender a log, just presenting part of the log or a day from the log can't be reliable if we don't have the rest of the log. If there's something concerning what was noted down at 3.10 Sunday evening, well, this might be followed by other information that is important that might support the document in question or might -- in order to tender logs, we believe, Mr. President, that the Prosecution must provide us with more information in order to give these operational logs a minimum of reliability. The following category of documents concerns the issue of war diaries. We don't know what a war diary is. I personally know because of my previous military experience what a war diary is. I could provide a definition on the basis of what I did when I was engaged in the military. But this has nothing to do with the debate. It's still necessary to know before admitting a war diary whether it was a diary that was drafted at the time of the events themselves; was it a diary that was kept after the events; or was it a corporal at the bottom of the command chain who established the war diary? What sources were used? Or was it a high-ranking officer? Or were instructions issued with regard to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. drafting of the diary? And once more, with regard to a war diary, incomplete entries or choosing one page and not the rest of the diary in our opinion greatly diminishes the reliability of the evidence being presented. Mr. President, I'll now address telephone intercepts. With regard to this topic, Mr. President, my colleague mentioned, I think, the AID or the Agency -- I don't have the term before me. But it was a secret body of the Ministry of the Interior, of the MUP. And they intercepted certain telephone conversations. When we examined the document tendered, Mr. President, we note that it's not as I thought up until yesterday, the interception of a conversation that was recorded on a tape; it's an electronic intercept. That is to say, in appearance -- apparently, it was someone who was listening to a conversation and took notes while listening to the conversation. So as far as reliability is concerned, Mr. President, this is very different from a telephone intercept for which we would have transcript, recorded on tape. We don't know why the Ministry of the Interior engaged in electronic surveillance, electronic intercepts in its own army. This is very important. This is a very important factor to be taken into account before such an intercept is admitted. It's necessary to provide many indicia of reliability for such proof presented by the Prosecution, proof concerning how the conversation was intercepted. We need proof about the reliability of the intercept. The person who was taking notes, was that person really in a position to hear the conversation? Were the notes handwritten? We don't know anything about the document itself. There's no stamp, no indication of its origin. Mr. President, this is the type of document that was obtained from the archives, and we believe, according to some documents, we have an electronic intercept, but we don't know anything about the context within which this conversation was recorded. The person speaking, were they actually identified? The conversation, the transcript of the conversation, was this really a conversation between the two persons mentioned in the document? We have no idea on the basis of the document itself about this. And this diminishes all the more the reliability of this document or the way in which the Trial Chamber could use such a document. And that is why tomorrow, we will be arguing that such a document makes it absolutely necessary for a witness to come to testify about such documents in order for such a document to be admitted into evidence. The question of videos, Mr. President, this is a question that we have already addressed earlier on in the proceedings. There are certain videos which have been proposed by the Prosecution. We are of the opinion, Mr. President, that the applicable rules to a videotape are of the rules that apply to material evidence. And within the framework of material evidence, physical evidence which is slightly different from the rules applicable to the production of documents, the indicia of reliability are even more important, and the standard of reliability has to be higher. Through videos, a representation is being produced which is allegedly in conformity with the truth about certain evidence. The proposed videos are accompanied by sound recordings, so with one document two things are sought after, to provide a representation of the truth regarding a series of events, and also a commentary on the events that are shown on that video. Regarding video evidence and reliability, we have to know who made the video, we need to know in what context the video was made, and we need additional proof so that it should have a minimum of reliability. If I go to the internet today, I could find several videos that are accessible which are propaganda videos produced by various associations. Those videos, Mr. President, we don't know who prepared them, how they prepared them, why they prepared them. Those documents have absolutely no reliability, especially in the case of a trial before an international tribunal. The video produced here by the Prosecution, some are propaganda videos which, in our submission, have no indicia of reliability and which may be used by the Chamber when judging the total proof provided. If a video is produced by an investigator of the OTP, we believe, and we'll come back to tomorrow, without having someone who can recognise that video, the video will not have any reliability, as we are asked to take as given a picture of which we don't know the source. And this was something that the Chamber raised. Finally, Mr. President, when we come to photographs, the same applies. We have several photographs that have been tendered by the Prosecution as admissible. All those photographs in our judgement were taken long after the events. An important index of reliability of a photograph is that it should have been taken at the time the event took place. A photograph taken ten days subsequent to the event has no indicia of reliability, and it cannot be of any use to the Chambers unless it is supported with additional evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, ten years, not ten days after the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When talking about photographs and videos of crime sites where crimes were allegedly committed, without knowing the source and without additional proof, these elements do not meet the criteria of minimum reliability, the prima facie proof of reliability which would allow those elements to be used. This completes the presentation of General Hadzihasanovic's Defence regarding the source. But as the Chamber has been able to note, we have focussed our presentation both on prima facie proof of reliability as well as on authenticity, which comes within the framework of reliability. We have also -- we also have some arguments to present regarding documents. If the Chamber wishes to hear those submissions, we have some specific documents that we should like to show and use by way of an example. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. The other Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. To add only a few points to what Mr. Bourgon has already covered very extensively, Your Honour, our basic submission is that the documents that the Prosecution proposes to introduce do not become more reliable simply because they have been collected or received in a proper manner by the Office of the Prosecutor or by some international organisation or grouping that has then handed the documents over to the Prosecution. What is important is what occurred before the documents were received by the Office of the Prosecutor. And in that regard, our fundamental point is that the Prosecution today have not offered any further evidence of the real source of the documents. That's both the documents that come from the archive of Bosnia and the other archives, and also in respect of the individual categories of documents that my learned friend from the Prosecution referred to. Your Honour, it is for that reason that we understand that Your Honours were interested when Your Honours set out the directions for this hearing, to find out from the Prosecution, especially in relation to the military documents and orders which are crucial for a case like this, a command-responsibility case, that Your Honours requested that information be provided about how those documents were prepared, how were they distributed, how were they received, and how were they used by the armed forces involved. In our submission, those elements are all crucial for determining the reliability of the document, especially so because this is a case that concerns commanders and what issues they ordered, what notice they had, what actions they took. I know, Your Honours, this is a matter that's to be addressed tomorrow, but the bottom line of all of this is that it appears that the Prosecution will not be able to provide that kind of information themselves, but that some witnesses will have to be called to address those issues. And it will be for the Prosecution, in our submission, to determine which are the most important documents for their case and which are the ones where witnesses are required. It is, of course, impossible to call a witness for every document. We will be here until next year. But it's a question of prioritising and proving the issues that are essential for proving the allegations of the Prosecution's case. In that regard, it is encouraging that the Prosecution has indicated that statements could be taken from the archivists for the different archives that were mentioned today. And in our submission, that would be an important first step to be taken in order to determine how documents in general were collated by the Bosnian Army. In respect of the 7th Brigade in particular, our main concern, and there's no secret about this, is that our understanding is that there was, in fact, no archive for the 7th Brigade in 1993 and for a long time thereafter. It is important for us to know how documents that were allegedly circulating within the 7th Brigade were, in fact, collected from 1993 onwards and kept in a central place. The obvious point being what were the potential avenues in which documents could have found their way into an archive and whether those are authentic and reliable documents. It was a war situation. Organisation of documents was not a priority. And we are most interested to know how documents were collated and, of course, what were the possibilities of contamination of those documents or documents arriving there that simply were never, ever part of the proper chain of command. The same could apply to the Bosnian archive, and likewise with the HVO archive, which was one that was not initially kept in Bosnia, but one that was gathered from Bosnia over a period of time and then transported to Zagreb. And to know how that process took place is also important in establishing whether the documents are reliable. So those statements from the archivists or other persons are important for us to establish at a general level how the documents were collated. And it may well be as occurred in the Stela and Tuta case that cross-examination of those witnesses will be necessary. But of course, that will be kept to whatever is absolutely essential in putting the Prosecution to the proof of their case. Moving from the general level, then, to the particular documents, Your Honours, beyond what evidence an archivist can give, in our submission, it would be necessary for evidence to be called in relation to particular documents of the Bosnian Army. There are a number of orders, reports - Your Honours would have seen these listed in the consolidated list - which are potentially relevant to the issues in this case. That's another matter which we're going to have to address separately. Some of those were allegedly signed by the accused, but many of them were not. They were signed by other parties. And the Defence is simply not in a position at this stage to say anything about whether those signatures are authentic; also, whether or not those orders were part of the operations of the different brigades, in Mr. Kubura's case, the 7th Brigade. And when it is quite clear that these documents were prepared allegedly by somebody and signed by somebody, in our view, it would be possible to call a witness to explain the document and to clarify how the document was prepared and where it was sent. So there's a limited category of Bosnian Army documents where the author or another witness could be called. In relation to the documents that were purportedly signed by Mr. Kubura, there are a few of these. We notice that there are some different signatures that have been used. For example, in the proposed Exhibit Number 8, there's a signature there that is very different to the other signatures which were used by Mr. Kubura. And in respect of those documents, and I can go through the details if Your Honours want more detail about that, we would require that further evidence be led on documents where the signature is different to the one used by Mr. Kubura. There are also documents that are signed on behalf of Mr. Kubura, which he didn't himself sign. There, again, we would need to know who was the person who signed those documents and hear evidence about when that document was prepared and how it was used. So Your Honours, we are looking both at the organisation of the army documents at a general level, but then we have to come down to particular documents, and especially documents prepared by third parties; in other words, not the accused. In our submission, it is essential in order to authenticate those documents that evidence is heard on them and that it's clarified exactly who prepared them and how they were then used within the chain of command. Turning to the particular categories, and I'm most grateful for Mr. Bourgon's explanation of all the various categories that we highlight when contesting a number of these documents, and I don't wish to repeat them. We support all the categories that he has raised. There are one or two additional ones that I did wish to mention. The first is that there are some documents that are on the list that have not been disclosed to us. For example, numbers 585 and 586, which are the district prosecutor's registers of cases that were brought in 1993 and 1994 in Travnik and Zenica. These are registers we haven't received yet. And in addition to that, we've already had a witness from the Travnik district military court, and the opportunity was not used at that time to introduce those registers. There are other examples of where both HVO witnesses and Bosnian Army witnesses have been called, and yet the opportunity has not been used to show those witnesses documents, even if they were not able to identify the particular document but to authenticate the form in which the document was used and to indicate information on the document which would show how it was sent, how it was received, what was the usual way in which documents passed through the chain of command. It is, of course, not too late. The Prosecution's case is still underway, and it is of course for the Prosecution to decide whether or not it wishes to use the opportunity to call evidence in order to seek to authenticate the documents that it wishes to rely upon. Then there's another category of documents which relates to witnesses who have been withdrawn by the Prosecution. And in our submission, some of those witnesses who are so-called insider witnesses who could have provided information about many of these documents, that those documents should not be admitted in a situation where the document was initially introduced because the witness was to testify and was to be one of the documents of that witness. If the witness is not called, in our view, another witness must be called in order to introduce that document.
