And this is especially the case if the witness who was withdrawn was, in fact, the author of the document. Then in our view, those documents should be withdrawn as the witness was withdrawn. Another category which Mr. Bourgon touched upon was that of exhibits in other cases. In our submission, Rule 92 bis could be used, but only in situations where the information contained in those documents did not comment upon the conduct and acts of the accused. As Your Honours will know, that is the test set out in Rule 92 bis. And from our examination, these documents do go directly to the acts of the accused, especially in the context of being charged for the alleged crimes of their subordinates. Your Honour, and lastly, this is a category that applies specifically to Mr. Kubura, and it might be one that goes to the issue of relevance, but I thought it useful to outline it now so that we know what the full parameters of the challenges brought by Mr. Kubura. There are a number of documents which are dated before the 1st of April 1993, and also after the last incident that he is charged with in Vares in November 1993. In our submission, these documents are to be excluded as falling outside of the time period of the indictment unless the Prosecution can show, and the onus is on the Prosecution, to show a clear link between those documents and the crime base within the period of the indictment when it is alleged that Mr. Kubura had command of the perpetrators. The Appeals Chamber decision on this point made it quite clear that a commander can only be charged for crimes committed while he has command of the alleged subordinates. It must be contemporaneous. And in our view, any documents falling outside of the period of command should be excluded unless relevancy can be shown, not at a general level, but it must be directly linked to the particular crimes that occurred and the time period when it is alleged the accused had command over subordinates for those crimes. The Prosecution has not set out in its document what the relevancy of any of these documents is, and we would, therefore, submit that they should be excluded. Indeed, the Prosecution has on a number of occasions itself submitted that documents that the Defence sought to introduce should be excluded because they were outside of the period of the indictment. I have one example here, Your Honours, which I can provide for Your Honours. On page 2571 of the transcript of 10 February 2004 where my learned friend Mr. Withopf objected to a document being introduced on the basis that because it was dated in October 1992, it is clearly outside the time frame of the present indictment and should be excluded. So the Prosecution has applied this standard to the Defence exhibits as well. Your Honours, this may be a question that has to be addressed further when we look at relevancy, but I raise it now for completeness to indicate all the objections that are made by Mr. Kubura. Those are our submissions at this stage. Your Honours, we can provide more details about specific documents if that is requested. I'm grateful, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Dixon. The Prosecution will respond to what has been said, but it will do so after the break, which we're going to have in a couple of minutes. In order to be fully informed about what has been said by Defence counsel, I'm going to summarise under their control what has been said. First of all, the Defence for General Enver Hadzihasanovic has quoted certain decisions that were rendered in the Tadic, Delalic, Brdjanin cases in order to address the question of reliability. The Prosecution will, of course, tell us their opinion in a moment. And in connection with reliability, Mr. Bourgon referred to the contents of an order that I have in front of me of the 15th of February 2002 in the Brdjanin case. In the comments made by Mr. Bourgon, I am referring to paragraph 18 of that decision which was not mentioned, and that paragraph with respect to reliability says the following: "The implicit requirement of reliability simply means that there must be sufficient indicia of reliability to create a presumption." And this paragraph refers to the Delalic ruling. The Defence did not quote from another decision dated the 16th of April 2002 in the Stakic case. That order entitled "order relative to the standards for the admission of evidence," regarding the question of reliability, paragraph 9, and I will simply quote from that paragraph. It is very brief, as you will see. "Regarding documentary evidence, the Chamber does not support the thesis according to which the question of reliability when raised has to be considered as a first stage in the presentation of evidence which is being tendered." There are certainly other decisions that were rendered, but it was necessary for me to add to the reference made to jurisprudence regarding reliability. Regarding reliability, the Defence requests that we establish fully the origin of the document, the chain of custody criteria, the date when a document was drafted, the date when it was produced, how it was kept, the criterion of authenticity, and also we have to see whether it could be considered to be false or suspect or uncertain as a document. Proceeding from all of these criteria, the Defence is requesting that these criteria be applied to different orders. The Defence referred to various sources. And in conclusion, virtually rejected all the sources. I'm going to leaf through those very quickly. When there is no source, it cannot be admitted. The documents from the Blaskic case should not be admitted. Concerning documents produced by witnesses, they should have been tendered when the witness was here. Therefore, they should be rejected. Regarding documents coming from a government, in that case, too, the same criteria should be applied. Regarding private sources, we have to know the source and the reason. As for documents coming from the 3rd Corps, the standard defined regarding reliability should be applied. As for documents external to the 3rd Corps or coming from outside the 3rd Corps, in that case, too, it is necessary to establish that the accused were aware of the existence of those documents. As for HVO documents, the Defence asks that they be rejected. As for logbooks, again, those logs should be viewed in totality, not excerpts from them. As for war diaries written on a daily basis, again, we have to know who wrote them, and we don't know them. If it's a corporal, of course it doesn't have the same Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. value as if it were a general. As for telephone intercepts, the Defence has referred to many points which I'm not going to repeat. When it comes to videos, again, the Defence naturally asks that they be rejected because they lack indicia of reliability. Rejected because they lack indicia of reliability. As for photos, as they were taken years later, they, too, should be rejected. As for General Kubura's Defence, Mr. Dixon presented different arguments, specifically the question of signature of General Kubura. There are different signatures, we are told. So we have a problem there. Then there are documents that are attributed to Mr. Kubura but were not signed by him. Therefore, there, too, we have a problem. Regarding the documents that could have been produced through witnesses and were not, Mr. Dixon asked that those documents be rejected. As for the possibility of calling evidence on the basis of 92 bis rule, Mr. Dixon tells us that this cannot be used if they refer directly to the acts and behaviour of the accused. And finally, the Defence through Mr. Dixon spoke of the question of time; that is, that documents should not be admitted that do not fit into the time period covered by the indictment. And the Defence in this connection referred to page 2.571 when the Prosecution requested that a document produced by the Defence be rejected on the ground that the document was drafted in 1992, which is outside the scope of the indictment. I have tried very quickly to summarise the submissions of the Defence. And the Prosecution after the break will, of course, present their arguments, and then we will go on to the second topic on our agenda. Yes, Mr. Bourgon. Theoretically, it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, a small observation, with your permission: The Chamber -- the president says that the reference to the jurisprudence was not complete that I made. With all due respect, I referred to points that were contrary to the submissions of the Prosecution. And I said that this -- that the arguments of the Defence were focussing on the fact that there need to be sufficient indicia of reliability. I wanted to properly inform the Chamber, providing both sides of the argument, and not only one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for that clarification. We will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, you may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I'm going to address a number of the issues raised by my learned friends from the Defence teams, and I'm going to address them to the extent possible, considering the time that has been passed by today. Allow me three introductory remarks. Although the Prosecution certainly understands that the issues that relate to the documents are to some extent intermingled, unfortunately my learned friends didn't follow the order of the issues as they should have been addressed today and tomorrow. The second introductory remark, Mr. President, authenticity, reliability, probative value and admissibility of documents are distinct issues, and they should be addressed distinctly. Sometimes, unfortunately, they were again mixed up. And the third introductory remark, Defence tendered on a number of occasions documents which by no means would match the criteria Defence today is asking the Trial Chamber to establish in respect to the proposed Prosecution exhibits. After these introductory remarks, let me please address a number of the issues, first of all, authenticity. We think it became reasonably clear in the course of the Prosecution's presentation why the Prosecution thinks their documents are authentic. They are authentic because the vast majority or the vast majority of the documents are authentic because they are official documents stemming from an official archive or from official archives, and the vast majority of such documents have official stamps on them. These are all features, Mr. President, Your Honours, the Trial Chamber has repeatedly made reference to in reaching decisions or providing guidance to the parties as to the issue of admissibility of documents. I understand there's an agreement between the parties that the archivists may be in a position to shed some additional light on these issues, and they may be in a position to provide a full picture, or at least portions of a full picture as to how the documents came into the archives, as to when, and maybe even to the extent what happened prior to the time they came to the respective archives. What the Prosecution, however, wishes the Trial Chamber draw particular attention to is a matter which hasn't been addressed by our learned friends from the Defence, and that's the issue of the totality of documents. A decision can only be made after the totality of documents, meaning all documents, have been looked at. And I'm in particular making reference to documents stemming from the military. It's the sequence of orders, reports back, following-up orders or not following-up orders which will play, or in the view of the Prosecution, should play, a crucial role in making a final determination about the admissibility of documents. Defence approach is to have an isolated view on the documents; the Prosecution's approach is, Mr. President, Your Honours, to have a look at the documents in their totality. In this context, we wish to raise an issue which has been addressed a number of times, and that's the issue of signatures. The Prosecution is very well aware that there are documents which contain signatures, signatures in quite a number of instances of the one or the other accused. Other documents, however, which have the name of the one or the other accused on them don't have their signatures. There must be a reason for it, and one of the reasons may be, and it has been addressed by my learned colleague from the Hadzihasanovic Defence, the manner these documents were produced and were sent. Once they were produced, they were signed by the one who was the person in charge to order. The one who received the order, the document, and in many instances, these orders were transferred using electronic, sophisticated electronic means, the one who received the document, this document doesn't have a signature on it. In this context, Mr. President, Your Honours, it may be helpful, it may be helpful, and the Prosecution will certainly put some effort on this issue, it may be helpful to identify which document was found in which binder. In using the materials the Prosecution was able to provide the Trial Chamber with, it is possible to a certain extent to establish whether a document was found in a binder that clearly shows that this was the receiving end or in a binder that clearly shows that this was the sender of the document. Further on in respect to signatures, the Prosecution, as Defence counsel are aware of, are in possession of original signatures of the accused and, of course, would be able to produce such original signatures if necessary; and if necessary, also to an expert. Another main issue, and I'm moving on to a different topic obviously, Mr. President, Your Honours, are the HVO documents. In our view, the Defence discussed to some extent issues which are more related to the evidentiary value, to the probative value of such documents, rather than to any issues related to their admissibility. HVO documents, as it is obvious, have been used in the so-called flipside cases before this Tribunal against Bosnian Croat accused, and HVO documents in such cases have been admitted into evidence. The admissibility of such documents, Mr. President, Your Honours, cannot depend on who the accused is. A document can either be reliable or it can't be reliable, but it is not an issue as to in which case, before which Trial Chamber a document is used. Defence has tendered quite a number of documents, and they were allowed to do so, and in the view of the Prosecution, it was the right decision to allow them to do so, has tendered documents which stem from the HVO or the HDZ. Such documents would certainly not match the criteria Defence tried to have the Trial Chamber establish for the Prosecution's proposed exhibits. If I may move on to particular issues, and I'm only addressing a selection of such issues, it is correct that there are documents and/or exhibits on the -- or videos on the Prosecution exhibit list which have been handed over in a few circumstances and a few instances by a witness who has already testified or by a few witnesses who have already testified before this Tribunal in the present case. The Prosecution, for a number of reasons, in such instances hasn't used the document and/or the videotape in examining the witness. Such instances include situations in which the witness was the person who was not able to comment on the document or the video for the reason that he got the video from somebody else. RFAs that have been addressed -- that the Prosecution should in respect to such documents it got from governments or other official authorities, that such documents which were the result of such requests for assistance, that the RFAs should be attached. Although the Prosecution is obviously in a position to do so, it would be a bit reluctant because such RFAs quite often also address issues which are or do fall under the umbrella of still-ongoing investigations. If the Trial Chamber wishes, however, the Prosecution to do so, such RFAs can be produced either on an ex parte basis or in a redacted version. Another issue that be addressed by my learned friends from the Defence, and this is the issue in respect to documents which do not stem from either the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade or directly from the 3rd Corps headquarters in Zenica. It's the Prosecution's view that all documents which either stem from any unit falling within the ABiH 3rd Corps area, area of responsibility, or any reports from such units are relevant, are potentially relevant to the indictment and to the charges in the indictment because they may reveal, and in the view of the Prosecution, they do reveal, issues related to command and control; and again, such orders quite often are part of a series of orders and reports, and that touches again on the issue of totality. And they may or they should only be seen together with any other orders touching on the very same issues. The war diaries have been addressed. It is correct, the war diaries have only been translated in portions, in portions into English. They are obviously in B/C/S. However, Defence is in possession of the full war diary. Therefore, Defence is obviously also in a position to address any issues that relate to times, time periods, either prior or after the day or the days the Prosecution is making reference to or wishes to go into further detail. I'm not sure on what basis my learned colleagues from the Defence try to discredit the Prosecution videos as propaganda videos. Unfortunately, we haven't been told the reasons why. The photographs, very briefly, they quite often have been used. They are mainly showing crime scenes. To date, this hasn't been issue at all. It's the first time that it has been addressed, today. One important issue has been discussed by my learned friend from the Kubura Defence. That's the issue of the time period of the indictment. And the Defence tries to limit the Prosecution to the crime-based incidents of the indictment, meaning from 28 -- 26 of January 1993 up until 3rd or 4th of November 1993. It is obvious from the indictment that the accused Kubura prior to becoming the acting commander was the chief of staff of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. Documents which show that the accused Kubura got to know about certain orders of his predecessor, Mr. Asim Koricic, of course are relevant because they touch upon the issue of knowledge, notice and knowledge. And this issue should not be intermingled with the Appeals Chamber decision. The Appeals Chamber decision touches on potential charges, but any issues related to notice and knowledge or other issues related to Article 7(3) of the Tribunal's Statute can still be covered, and such documents in the view of the Prosecution can be tendered. On the other end of the time frame, Mr. Kubura was far longer than until the 4th of November 1993 the commander of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. And the responsibility and the duty to punish, Mr. President, Your Honours, doesn't end at the point in time the last crime was committed; the duty and the responsibility to punish continues at the very least until the point in time or until the point in time the accused, based on his command position, had the opportunity, and not only the opportunity but the duty and the responsibility, to do so. These very same issues obviously apply also to the accused Hadzihasanovic. There are a number of documents which are outside the indictment period. Quite often, they have to do with the establishment of the 3rd Corps. Quite often, they have to do with the establishment of other military units which at a later point in time, as it is shown in the indictment, were involved in crimes which do form part of the indictment. Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the time being, these are the comments the Prosecution wishes to make to the observations of our learned friends from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It's not necessary to engage in additional discussions at this point in time. Perhaps certain issues will be addressed on the basis of the themes that are yet to come. The second subject concerns the technical problems that relate to the documents. Mr. Withopf, you may now address this second theme.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the technical problems are mainly related to two main issues addressed by the Defence. Number one are any issues related to translations; and number two are issues related to disclosure of proposed exhibits. And there's a third issue which has been addressed by the Trial Chamber on Friday last week. That's the poor quality of the photocopies. If I may start to address the very last issue first, there are a number of reasons why the photocopies appear to be of a poor quality. And the main reason, Mr. President, Your Honours, is the fact that the originals, that the originals which were photocopied were of poor quality. Unfortunately, the photocopy can't make the original any better. This particular issue is to some extent also addressed in the declaration of Mr. Robert Reid which was handed over earlier today. I may please refer to the respective portion in his declaration. Issues of disclosure, the Prosecution has, always has made, and continues to make, and on a regular basis is successful in doing so, to fulfil its disclosure obligations, and we will continue to do so. Whatever document or other proposed exhibit may not have been disclosed, and if one considers the amount of the materials, only very few materials are obviously missing, we will take care of it and will make them available at the very earliest opportunity. The third issue, this appears to be the most important issue, and I think that's probably the view of both the Defence and the Prosecution. This is the issue of translations. Prior to going into any further details, I think I should provide the Trial Chamber some sort of overview what sort of translations do exist and do form part of the materials that have been provided as proposed exhibits. There are four different types of translations. Number one are the fully CLSS-certified translations. Number two are draft translations which are usually indicated as such. They were done by CLSS; however, are not yet certified. And then we have translation and again are indicated as such, which are called REV translations. REV stands for "rough English version." It's actually not what it says since the REV translations are full, full translations of a document. The difference to the CLSS-certified translations is the following: REV translations were done by the investigations team language assistants which are qualified for such translations, who are, however, not working within CLSS. Therefore, such translations don't have the, if I may call it, official certification of CLSS. I wish, however, to emphasise that such translations are full translations of the full respective document. And finally, Mr. President, Your Honours, we have what's called summary translations. These are what it actually says. Such translations are summarising the document, some to a limited extent, others to an extent which is close to a full translation. There are, obviously, REV translations and summary translations, and the latter ones appear to be the most problematic ones. The Prosecution will make efforts to replace the summary translations, and there are not many of them to, replace such summary translations by full either REV or, if possible, by CLSS certified translations. These are the three issues, Mr. President, Your Honours, I wish to address at this point in time. There may be other issues I may address after Defence has been given the opportunity to raise their or to make their observations. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. Regarding the technical problems linked to the documents, you have addressed three points, the poor quality of the photocopies, the obligation of disclosing to the Defence the documents that you have, and questions linked to translation. Regarding the technical problems of the documents, I will give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Before starting to address the submissions of the Defence linked to technical problems, I should simply like to make a clarification regarding the position of the Defence with respect to all the documents that the Prosecution wishes to tender into evidence. The position of the Defence is not that all the documents proposed and contested should not be admitted and that they can never be admitted into evidence. The position of the Defence, Mr. President, is that these documents could perhaps be admitted into evidence, but not at this stage. That is the position of the Defence. The constant element emanating from the jurisdiction -- jurisprudence which is rather surprising to me and it is only quite recently that I fully understood the mechanism emanating from several decisions. There's a Rule 89(C) which requires also an indicia of reliability inherent to the probative value and to relevance. And we're also told that these indicia of reliability is not the first test and not the first stage. According to certain decisions, this is prima facie proof of reliability. And that depends on the four criteria that I mentioned earlier on. Therefore, when a document meets the indicia of reliability, the Defence is not opposed to their admission. And many documents proposed by the Prosecution could meet the indicia of reliability, but not at present. Having said that, the Defence has very little to add. The principal question is to see whether we can read the documents in their entirety for them to be reliable at first glance. If the photocopy is such that we can't even see the contents of a document, then that is not so. If half of a document is blackened out and only half is legible, then this cannot be a reliable document, as it is incomplete. Also, the same applies when it comes to the question of signatures. As I have already said, for us a signature is a test of reliability. But if the signature is illegible, that's a technical problem. Can the signature be recognised? If yes, then there's no technical problem there. The problem of translation, Mr. President, is linked to the fact that the translation of documents has to be a faithful translation of the whole document. Therefore, documents accompanied with a translated summary in the opinion of the Defence cannot be admitted as such. I think that my learned friend is -- appreciates this. And he realises that these documents need to be fully translated for them to be able to be admitted without any technical problem. Regarding the use of translations which may be certified translations by the CLSS or those marked with REV, we feel that the standard that should be used should be that for the admission of evidence. Therefore, if we admit a document without going through a witness or through some other means, the standard that that document needs to meet in terms of translation has to be almost perfect so that to make sure that a document that is admitted must be exact and reliable. Whereas if a document is produced through a witness, even if the translation is not perfect, but we have to use nonverified or noncertified translation, we regret to have to do that. I think that applies to all parties. But due to financial constraints and other reasons, we have to do so sometimes. However, if we have a witness who can assist us with a document, then such a translation is perhaps acceptable. However, if a document is being produced without a witness for the value of the document itself, then for it to be admissible we need to have a complete translation and a certified translation of that document. And a final element concerning technical problems is the problem Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of markings that appear on documents and -- of which we don't know the origin. In the document that we filed with the Chamber, we identified three types of markings on documents. Sometimes there may be handwritten notes on the document. Or parts of the document which were underlined, or there are parts of the document which were highlighted. And we don't know, Mr. President, who added those notes and those markings on the document. And these markings are very important for the evaluation that the Chamber will make of those documents. So we need to know who modified those documents because if a note is added at the bottom of a document, one could go as far as to say that this was a different document. By way of example, there's a document sent by the 3rd Corps commander to the headquarters of the army in Sarajevo. The army commander receives that document. He adds a note on it and distributes the document for action within his headquarters. We no longer have one document, but we have two documents. We have an initial communication from the corps commander to the army command followed by a second communication between the army commander and somebody else within his headquarters or his staff. Such notes need to be explained. Otherwise, the Chamber may have a document which it is unable to understand without additional evidence. So this is a technical problem which in our view merits further clarification through additional evidence so that the document in its present condition can be reliable. If a document receives -- if a commander receives a document and then underlines certain parts of it, this could lead the Chamber to believe that this part of the document was considered to be more important than the rest of the document by the person who received it. So if we don't know who underlined the document, the Chamber cannot know who it is that thought that this part of the document was more important. Therefore, we need additional information so that the Chamber may use those documents. Without such information, the indicia of reliability are insufficient for admitting a document. I will stop there regarding technical problems. But I would simply like to add a final remark concerning the signature procedure. My learned friend addressed this topic at the beginning of his submissions by saying that the Defence of General Hadzihasanovic indicated that maybe it could be an electronic document or a document maybe signed by someone who authorises the order. The problem, Mr. President, is that we don't have that information, and that information can only be provided by the Prosecution through evidence to show what the procedure was within the headquarters. Who was authorised to sign? Who was authorised to draft? And who was authorised to press the button to distribute this document bearing the signature of a particular commander? For this reason, Mr. President, we feel such documents need additional proof to meet the requirement for indicia of reliability. And my final remark refers to HVO documents. HVO documents could become admissible, Mr. President. What we are saying, our argument is that the more removed a document is from the accused, the higher the standard needs to be regarding reliability. If it's a document that has nothing to do with the accused, and we wish to use it against him, then it is even more important that it be reliable and that we have proof of the signature, the sender, and the receiver. And when talking about the two other topics, I will be able to give you two very precise and concrete examples from which we see that without additional proof, those documents do not meet the indicia of reliability sufficient for admission. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. I turn now to Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. When Your Honours outlined the areas that were to be addressed under this topic, the one that Your Honours indicated was the question of unsigned documents. In that regard, the Prosecution was requested to clarify how it was that certain documents were unsigned, and we have been given one explanation today, that it could be because of the manner in which the document was sent. However, as Your Honours noted in the transcript when this issue was identified, it could also be because they were duplicate copies and duplicate copies might have been kept on file or they might have been sent to other persons. There might be other reasons why a document was unsigned. Most importantly, from the Defence's point of view, the document might not in fact have been sent, and Your Honours might in that situation give limited probative value to a document which might have been prepared by one of the accused, signed but never sent anywhere. It's not in our submission evidence that the Prosecution can give from the bar table as to what happened to various documents. It is a matter which has to be addressed by evidence directly from the witness. It might be that somebody from the Office of the Prosecutor can answer this question, but then a statement has to be prepared and that person made available for cross-examination. The second area Your Honours identified was illegible signatures. Your Honours might think that this is the most important part of a document, whether or not it has been signed and whether or not it's clear who signed the document. Your Honours indicated that that would have to be clarified, and with the greatest of respect to my learned friends from the Prosecution that is another matter which hasn't been specifically made any clearer today through their submissions. Where signatures are illegible, it might be because of photocopying; it might be for other reasons. But an explanation must be given in our view. Otherwise, the documents should not be admitted. And the final area Your Honours identified was that of handwritten documents. There are a number of handwritten documents which have no stamps on them. They are not official documents, as my learned friend has attempted to put emphasis on the official status of stamps and government documents. But there are many which have no record from an official body on the document. And here, Your Honours indicated that you wish to know to what extent these documents were in the official archives, which archive. And as Your Honours say, once again, who wrote them. That information in our submission has not been provided today by the Prosecution. So Your Honours, on the topic of technical matters, these are three areas which we wish to highlight which have not been addressed, and the documents that fall into those categories as identified in our list, we submit, should not be admitted. As a final point, Your Honours, of course it is always open to Your Honours to admit these documents on the basis that they are documents which were obtained from archives or they are documents which are part of the Prosecution case, and yet attach very little weight to them because of the problems that have been identified. But in our view, it would be a better course to look at what probative value could be attached to these documents when considering whether they should be admitted or not. And the test that we have outlined is that they should be of some assistance to Your Honours before they are admitted into the body of evidence of this case. If they are of limited assistance on their own or standing together with other documents, in our view, they should be excluded at this stage. Or they could be given numbers for identification, as has happened, and they could be admitted at a later stage if through other evidence being laid in the Prosecution case they assume a greater reliability and a value which could assist Your Honours in deciding the ultimate issue of guilt or innocence in the case. But in our view, it is of limited purpose for the documents to be admitted when, in fact, they have little probative value and little weight in the end that could be attached to them in any event. I'm grateful, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, Mr. President. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before adjourning for the day, I shall give the floor again to the Prosecution so that they might respond to the problems raised, especially the last one which may be a bit surprising, and that is that the probative value should be assessed before a document is admitted. Mr. Withopf, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, if I may please very briefly address a number of issues which have been raised by my learned friends from the Defence. Again, I wish to really emphasise that this is a circumstantial case. At the end of the day, there will be many, many, many bits and pieces of evidence which put together will provide the Trial Chamber with the full picture, the full picture of the truth. What's on the face of the documents or of a document being looked at in isolation may appear to -- not to be relevant or not to be related to the present case. Once having considered the totality of the documents, this may look very different and such document or documents may become of certain, if not a high probative value. This is really a point we wish to again make at this junction. Markings of documents were addressed. It is correct, on a number of occasions there are such markings on documents. These markings I can sure were on the originals. They were obviously not made, and I understand the Defence is not suggesting that, they were not made by anybody from the Prosecution. We're obviously not in a position to -- at this point in time to explain who made the markings. I wish, however, to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber that the very same issue has been discussed only recently when Defence tendered into evidence a document which had significant portions of markings or highlighted portions, and if my recollection isn't wrong, I think to recall that this document was actually tendered into evidence. Again, the very same threshold should apply to both parties of these proceedings. Illegible signatures, it's certainly true that there are a number of documents which appear to have illegible signatures. At this point in time, there's not much to do about. We will, however, try to find any avenue which may lead to a resolution of this issue. Authorisation to sign documents or the internal procedures applied by the ABiH and, in particular, applied by the ABiH 3rd Corps, the internal ABiH regulations which contain to some extent information on how such documents were produced and/or transmitted will be of some assistance to determine this issue. Again, the probative value, as has been repeatedly mentioned by the Trial Chamber, has nothing to do with the issue of the admissibility of documents, and what we are discussing in the course of the today's and the tomorrow's proceeding is the issue of the admissibility and nothing else. Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We need to adjourn. The Chamber notes that on the three topics on the agenda, one hasn't been addressed; that is relevance. Then there's the two other, 89(D) and the documents which necessarily need to be admitted through a witness. We said that we would see today whether on Thursday the witness planned could be heard. Everything will depend now on the time that will be needed by Mr. Withopf tomorrow to address the three other points and the time that the Defence counsel plans to take. So Mr. Withopf, can you give us some indication regarding tomorrow and do you think that tomorrow we will have finished the debate which would allow you to call your witness for Thursday, or do you feel already now that this witness should be postponed to another date?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I think that it's still possible to hear the witness on the Thursday. Since the three issues to be discussed tomorrow are to some extent limited in their scope, and the Prosecution's submissions will certainly not take as much time as they have taken today, so in the view of the Prosecution it's still likely that we can finish the discussion on the documents tomorrow. And the Prosecution will continue to work on the basis that the witness can be called on Thursday. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. Mr. Bourgon, do you think that we will cover everything tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, tomorrow my colleague is right in saying that the submissions will be shorter. Nonetheless, the Defence intends to present documents and to discuss the documents themselves to apply what we pleaded today. So I think that it would be difficult to cover all our documents in a single day, though we will do our best to reduce the number. But I think it will be very difficult to complete this work in one day. Having said that, Witness Morsink - I mention name though we're not in a private session, but that witness has not asked for any protective measures, he's an international witness. This witness will certainly require a whole day of hearing for his testimony. So if we pass our -- if we do not complete everything tomorrow and have to continue on Thursday, then it's a risk of not completing the witness on Thursday. So we would prefer to have a decision today to the effect that we call off the testimony of Mr. Morsink. Because if we have the witness on Thursday, we have to prepare today already, and this is rather complicated. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're of the opinion that it would be better to postpone Mr. Morsink's testimony to a later date. This view of the fact that you wish to produce documents tomorrow and discussing them today on the basis of the submissions you made today, how many documents do you intend to produce as an indication, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, 40 documents. But we can try and reduce that number. There are 40 documents that illustrate all the situations that we referred to today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So with respect to the criteria and the observations made, you have 40 documents that will illustrate your -- the points you made. I will give the floor to Mr. Withopf. But first, Mr. Dixon, we would also like to hear your opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. We also wish to introduce some documents by way of example. Because in our view, it's very difficult to look at these documents in pure categories. There are certain documents which we wish to identify to show why the document should be excluded, which might apply to other documents as well. And we would need to show about 15 to 20 of those as examples. And we think that is the only way we can move the process forward. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which means that we will be having a debate on at least 60 documents. And if we have a debate on 60 documents, and if one documents takes five minutes, 5 times 60, that's 300 minutes, which means five hours. I think that we can hardly expect to hear the witness on Thursday. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, may we please make a few suggestions. It would be very helpful and it would certainly accelerate the tomorrow's proceedings if the Defence today could indicate which documents they wish to address specifically tomorrow. If Defence counsel tell us now, we would obviously be in a far better position to prepare and to address any of the issues on short notice in comparison to a situation that a document out of the several hundreds of documents will be shown tomorrow, and it may require the Prosecution doing some additional inquiries. So I would suggest that the Defence in order to accommodate the wish of the Trial Chamber to not waste court time today, immediately after the court session, provides the Prosecution with the numbers of the documents they wish to use tomorrow. A second suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: If I may make a second suggestion, we would suggest that the witness, and the witness is already here in Holland, that the witness can be called as -- on Thursday, and we may continue during the afternoon on Thursday in order to complete the testimony of this witness. And the last issue or the last suggestion, we could again do the examination-in-chief, at least the examination-in-chief. Mr. President, Your Honours, for your information, the witness is a Dutch witness. That's the reason why he is already in Holland. He is with NATO usually in Germany, quite often requested to travel in Italy. However, he is basically at home in Holland. And for that reason, completely unrelated to his testimony, which is scheduled for Thursday, he is in Holland. If the Trial Chamber may please consider the suggestions made by the Prosecution, in particular suggestion one, that the Defence informs the Prosecution which documents they wish to have specifically discussed in the course of the tomorrow's proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are several problems. First of all, there are some 60 documents. And if the Defence tells the Prosecution the numbers of those 60 documents, it would allow the Prosecution to prepare. And also if the Prosecution gives the list of 60 documents to the legal officer of the Chamber, that would also be useful for the Chamber because, as you fully understand, when you produce a document tomorrow, we also have to see the document, which means pick up the binder, look through them. We only have one set of binders. We have to pass the document from one judge to another. This would take time. Therefore, regarding the idea of the Prosecution that they be told which documents will be used, this appears to be a good solution. A second point is that the Prosecution would like to at least begin the examination-in-chief on Thursday, which would mean that the cross-examination would be delayed. This is not so inconvenient as the witness being a Dutchman hasn't crossed the Atlantic to come here and testify for the cross-examination. So this is a possible solution. A third solution would be extra time, like in football, and I think this is linked to private obligations of each one of us. I have none. But it may be difficult for us to prolong the hearing to Thursday afternoon. We will make extensions, but we'll do that on another day. So the Defence should provide the Prosecution with a list of documents they intend to use tomorrow so that the Prosecution can prepare. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The idea of the Prosecution is certainly a good one. The only difficulty is that I mentioned 40. I was a bit optimistic because if I was to give a list to the Prosecution straight away, maybe there would be twice as many. To reduce them to 40 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber was sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but to reduce the list, I have to discuss the matter with my colleagues. So it is possible to give a list, but perhaps later, about 7.00 p.m. when we will be able to give the Prosecution this list. And to the Chamber as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But unfortunately, the Prosecution doesn't intend to be kept awake all night examining the documents, so we do have a problem. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can provide the short list to the Prosecution later on this afternoon, and also to your learned legal officer as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, sir. In such conditions, the witness scheduled for Thursday should be on standby. And depending on the problems that arise, we will either be in a position to commence with the examination-in-chief, and we will then not have any significant problems. Or if we're not in a position to examine the witness, we will postpone the witness's hearing. It would be more complicated if the witness lived elsewhere. But since the witness is Dutch and is in this country, the risk of the witness spending the weekend here is not that important given that we'll have an international witness who will be here on Friday. So the risk is quite slight. Mr. Bourgon, is there anything you wanted to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The other thing I wanted to add concerns extra time on Thursday afternoon. This would be difficult for the Defence because we already have other engagements that concern the expert witness who will be here on Monday. To the extent that it is possible, we would like to avoid splitting up the examination-in-chief from the cross-examination because the cross-examination can't -- will not be able to take place before two weeks. And he is an ECMM witness who is quite important. And we want to avoid having the cross-examination at a later time. If we split the procedure into two parts, this has certain advantages, but there are certain disadvantages for the presentation of evidence, both for the Trial Chamber and for the Defence when preparing its case. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have just deliberated, as you see. Given what you have said, we believe that it would be best to cancel the witness scheduled for Thursday. The witness will appear on some other date. And as I said, in June we could have an extension of time because there might be witnesses who will be appearing in June because some witnesses haven't been in a position to be heard. According to the schedule that we have, we have a schedule for May. But there are days that we have in June for witnesses. So this witness can either appear in May or in June. That's quite possible. We have to deal with -- we have to conclude the discussion of these documents. And in the Trial Chamber's opinion, continuing on Thursday should allow us to save time. We will now adjourn. I will see you all tomorrow at 9.00 to continue with the debate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 28th day of April, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
